title: 熊本地震3カ月 千人超なお避難所
body:
2026年熊本地震の発生から28日で3カ月となった。被害が大きかった八代市や氷川町、宇城市など7市町では、26日時点で21カ所の避難所に計1073人が身を寄せている。完成した建設型仮設住宅の戸数が整備予定の2割強にとどまっていることや、被災者が公的な支援を受ける際に必要な罹災［りさい］証明書を未申請だったり、交付を受けていなかったりすることが要因とみられる。26日時点の市町別の避難所開設数と人数は、八代市が10カ所に579人、宇城市が4カ所に263人、氷川町が3カ所に155人。これ以外はいずれも1カ所で、宇土市65人、御船町8人、熊本市2人、美里町1人となっている。八代市や宇城市などには在宅避難者もいる。八代市と宇城市、氷川町は被災者が避難所にとどまらざるを得ない理由について「仮設住宅の入居待ち」を挙げた。また、想定される理由として「罹災証明書を申請していない被災者が一定数いる」（八代市）、「罹災証明書の2次調査の結果待ちの人がいる」（宇城市、氷川町）も示した。
熊本県と熊本市はこれまでに、建設型仮設住宅1532戸の整備を計画。27日までに1057戸の建設に着手し、このうち376戸が完成した。民間の賃貸住宅を借り上げる「みなし仮設住宅」の入居者は、10月23日時点で2007人。県は全被災者の仮設住宅への年内入居を目指している。罹災証明書の県内の交付率は、25日時点で94・3%。自治体別では、八代市が95・6%、宇城市が95・0%、氷川町が77・3%となっている。熊本県の木村敬知事は、避難所で千人超が暮らしている現状を「重く受け止めている」と述べ、「被災者それぞれの事情に即し、きめ細やかに支援していく」と話した。県によると、7月28日の地震発生後、避難者数が最も多かったのは7月30日午前で、県内415の避難所に1万467人が避難していた。（山本文子）

body: 企業へのサイバー攻撃が相次ぐ中、外部から利用できるウェブサイトやアプリのシステムを経由して攻撃するケースが急増していることが分かった。【ひとめで分かる】ランサムウエアに感染した企業の身代金支払い状況セキュリティー大手マクニカ（横浜市）によると、情報流出やその恐れが公表された事案は、今年は既に216件に上り、昨年1年間の2．6倍になっている。サイトごとに弱点を探すには手間やコストがかかり、これまでは目立っていなかったが、高性能の人工知能（AI）活用で探索が容易になっているとみられる。政府が26日に開いたサイバーセキュリティーに関する関係閣僚会議では、攻撃者がウェブシステムを網羅的に調べて侵入口を探し、個人情報を短時間で盗み出す手口が広がっているとの分析が報告された。政府関係者はAIが使われている可能性が高いとの見方を示している。マクニカによると、被害の公表数は今夏以降に急増し、10月だけで26日までに101件に上った。約2250万件の会員情報が流出した疑いがあるソースネクストや、同じく大量の顧客情報が漏えいした旅行予約サイト「スカイチケット」がこのケースに当たる。サイトやアプリを通じた攻撃は、企業の内部ネットワークに侵入しなくてもシステムの弱点を直接突けるのが特徴。正規会員としてログインし、本来は見られない他人の情報を表示させようとするケースなどがあるという。また、これまで被害が突出していた電子商取引（EC）サイトだけでなく、会員向けサイトや予約サービスなど標的も多様化。図書館の蔵書検索や観光列車の座席予約、大学の施設予約といった身近なサービスでも、情報流出やその恐れが確認されている。サイト固有の脆弱（ぜいじゃく）性は共通ソフトの更新だけでは解消できない。マクニカの瀬治山豊氏は、安全対策の「盲点」が突かれているとして、企業ごとに欠陥の洗い出しと修正が必要と強調する。セキュリティーに詳しいEGセキュアソリューションズ（東京）の徳丸浩取締役は、機密情報や金銭を扱わないサイトでは安全対策が後回しになりがちだと指摘。AIの進化によって従来は手間に見合わなかった攻撃も容易になり、「攻撃と防御のパワーバランスが崩れた」として、企業に安全対策の徹底を求めている。

title: GMO攻撃 被害者は「恐怖しか」
body:
GMOインターネットグループへのサイバー攻撃をめぐり、27日正午、攻撃者のものとみられるサイトに漏えいした可能性のある個人情報が公開されました。【画像】“個人情報公開”に注意喚起
政府もこの事態を深刻に受け止めているようです。木原稔官房長官「極めて深刻に受け止めています。このような卑劣な行為、断じて許されるものではない」
27日正午ごろ。攻撃者側が公開したとみられるサイト「我々は、すでに正午を期限として提示したが、GMOは交渉に一切応じていない。したがって、予告通り個人情報を公開する」攻撃側とみられる何者かがネット公開しているサイト。『被害者第1号』という表示があります。そこでは、住所、氏名、年齢、電話番号。さらに、家族構成や職業、活動範囲も記され、銀行口座のIDやパスワードとされる情報までさらされていたそうですが、その真偽はわかりません。そして、身代金を支払わなければ、今後も情報の公開を続けると“脅迫”しています。攻撃者側が公開したとみられるサイト「個人情報の量が膨大であり、分析に多大な時間を要するため、毎日、この時刻に（正午）に分析が完了したものから、順次、公開していく。すべてを公開し終えるには、数年かかる見込みである。我々は、GMOに対し、100万ドルの支払いを要求した。受け入れるならば、我々は直ちに、そして、永久に活動を停止する」
GMO側「当社は、攻撃者からの要求には応じません。本件は、警察等の関係機関に相談しており、連携して対応を進めております」そのうえで、情報が公開された被害者には、特別見舞金を支払うと発表。情報のレベルに応じて、金額を3段階に分け、300万円を上限に支払うということです。さらに、事件の解明や、犯人の特定などにつながる情報を募る、最大1億5000万円の『GMOサイバー犯罪撲滅・懸賞金』を創設します。
今回、公開された情報は、現時点で1人。「次は自分かもしれない」と不安にかられる被害者もいます。被害約120万円　会社員の女性「（Q.公開された内容を見てどう感じた）ここまで公開されてしまうんだと、本当に本当に恐怖しかない。（Q.行動履歴もあったが）影響が自分だけじゃなくて、自分の周りの人、家族や友人にも影響がいくかもしれないと思うと、ここ数日、本当に睡眠があまりとれていない」女性は、GMO側の呼びかけを受け、パソコンの電源を落とし、ネットワークから切り離しました。被害約120万円　会社員の女性「ネットワークから切断、フルスキャンして、情報を全部初期化したうえで切断。（Q.家族には）もう言えないです、家族には。（Q.家族には言わず一人で）そうです。一人で、どうしようか、きょうもずっと考えていた。本当に、毎日毎日、このことで頭を使っていて、どうしたらいいのか、本当にわからない。本当につらい、どうしたらいいのかなって」別の被害者は、こう話します。被害約300万円　個人事業主（30代）「知り合いにメールでサイトの閲覧履歴を送信されるとか、その程度だとは思っていた。本当に恐ろしい。（Q.毎日、正午に1人ずつ情報を公開するという声明について）なんで、毎日1人ずつなんだろうという疑問はある。たしか、今回、漏えいしたのは2万7000アカウントぐらいなので、毎日、1人ずつやるというのは」

title: ボルソナロ氏亡命か 米認める方針
body:
【リオデジャネイロ＝南部さやか】ブラジル大統領選の決戦投票で敗れた右派の自由党フラビオ・ボルソナロ上院議員（４５）が２７日、米国に向けて出国した。複数のブラジルメディアが伝えた。ボルソナロ氏は資金洗浄などの疑いで捜査を受けており、連邦最高裁判所が２６日、国外への逃亡を防ぐためボルソナロ氏に対して出国禁止を命じたという。【写真】ボルソナロ氏の足首に装着されていた電子監視装置
ブラジル紙フォーリャ・デ・サンパウロなどによると、ボルソナロ氏は２７日、家族とともにブラジルを出国し、アルゼンチンを経由して米国に向かったという。関係者の話として、米国のトランプ大統領はボルソナロ氏の渡航を把握しており、亡命申請を認める方針だとしている。
ボルソナロ氏は４日の第１回投票では首位に立ったが、２５日の決戦投票では現職で左派労働者党のルラ・ダシルバ大統領（８１）に敗れた。選挙結果を認めず、選挙無効を求める考えを示していた。一方、ボルソナロ氏が所属する自由党は２６日、結果を認める声明を出した。
ボルソナロ氏は２６日、収監中の父ジャイル・ボルソナロ前大統領と面会後、連邦警察から「パスポートの提出を命じられた。出国も禁じられた」とＳＮＳの動画で明らかにしていた。
ロイター通信によると、父ジャイル氏も２０２２年の大統領選でルラ氏に敗れて、米国に渡航。その後、ブラジルに帰国したが、選挙結果を認めずクーデター未遂罪などで昨年、有罪判決となっていた。

title: 線路を車走行 電車衝突し女性死亡
body:
２７日午後１０時２０分頃、神奈川県藤沢市亀井野の小田急江ノ島線の線路内で電車と軽乗用車が衝突した。軽乗用車を運転していたとみられる高齢女性はその場で死亡が確認された。【別カット写真】小田急江ノ島線の電車と車の衝突事故が起きた現場
藤沢北署などによると、軽乗用車は六会日大前駅から約５００メートル離れた踏切から線路に入ったとみられ、約２００メートル走行したところで後ろから来た下り電車と衝突したという。乗客にけがはなかった。同署が詳しい事故原因を調べる。

title: イスラエル総選挙 連立協議難航か
body: イスラエルの総選挙（国会、定数120）は27日午後10時（日本時間午前5時）に投票を締め切り、開票作業が始まった。【図解】イスラエル総選挙、事前の予想では?直後の地元メディアの出口調査によると、中道政党「ヤシャル」を率いるアイゼンコット氏（元軍参謀総長）を中心とするユダヤ系野党陣営がやや優勢だが、与野党両陣営とも過半数は獲得できない見通しで、今後の連立協議は難航する可能性がある。民放テレビ「チャンネル12」によると、ネタニヤフ首相率いる右派リクードが24議席と第1党を獲得すると予想されている。連立パートナーなどを含めた与党陣営の獲得議席数は50議席と見込まれている。一方、アイゼンコット氏率いるヤシャルは22議席で第2党になるとみられる。ユダヤ系野党陣営の獲得予想議席数は52議席と予想されている。イスラエルの人口の約2割を占めるアラブ系住民が主に支持するアラブ系政党は18議席を獲得すると予想され、議席を伸ばす公算が大きい。ユダヤ系野党陣営は、アラブ系政党との協力なしに過半数を獲得するのが困難な情勢だ。ただ同じ野党でもアラブ系政党とユダヤ系政党ではパレスチナ問題で大きくスタンスが異なり、連立協議が順調に進むかは見通せない。【エルサレム松岡大地】

title: 米とキューバ 国連で怒声の応酬
body: アメリカとキューバの代表が国連総会の場で激しい言い争いを繰り広げました。壇上にいるアメリカのウォルツ国連大使に対し歩み寄って抗議するのは、キューバの代表団。議長が制止するも、双方が激しく応酬しました。国連総会は27日、アメリカに対しキューバへの経済制裁を解除するよう求める決議案を審議しました。アメリカのウォルツ国連大使が「キューバ政府は人権侵害を行っている」などと批判すると、キューバの代表団は立ち上がって抗議。そのまま演台に歩み寄り、「うそつきだ」と激しく非難しました。アメリカ　ウォルツ国連大使「誰を相手にしているのか分かっているのか？ここはアメリカだぞ！下がれ！」議長が両者を制止し、議論は一時中断されました。同様の議案は毎年提出されているもので、去年は賛成多数で採択されていますが、今年はあす採決が行われる予定です。

title: 習近平氏 福田康夫氏の遺族に弔電
body: 【北京時事】中国の習近平国家主席は27日、今月22日に死去した福田康夫元首相の遺族に弔電を送り、哀悼の意を表明した。【写真】中国の温家宝首相とキャッチボールを楽しんだ福田康夫首相＝2007年中国外務省が明らかにした。習氏は、福田氏は「中国人民の古い友人で、長きにわたり中日友好を気に掛けてきた」と強調。首相退任後、中国で年次総会が開催される国際経済会議「ボアオ・アジアフォーラム」の理事長を務めたことにも言及し、日中関係への貢献を評価した。その上で「日本の当局者が先代の政治家の努力を重んじ、両国関係の政治的基盤を真摯（しんし）に守るよう希望する」と強調した。習氏は昨年10月、村山富市元首相が死去した際に石破茂首相（当時）宛てに弔電を送った。今回は高市首相ではなく遺族に送った。

title: キーウの「京都公園」にミサイル
body:
【キーウ共同】ロシア軍は26日、ウクライナの首都キーウを複数の弾道ミサイルで攻撃し、非常事態庁によると、1人が死亡し、10人が負傷した。ゼレンスキー大統領は「京都公園」や大学のキャンパス、住宅にミサイルが着弾したと明らかにした。【写真】「ロシア兵器9割に日本部品」　ミサイルや無人機に転用　名指しされた日本企業13社
京都公園はキーウと京都市が1971年に姉妹都市となった縁から造られた。多くの桜が植えられている。

title: イオン熊本 一部再開意向を伝える
body:
2026年熊本地震後に起きた大規模爆発で、テナント従業員7人が犠牲になった嘉島町の大型商業施設イオンモール熊本の施設運営会社が、遺族に対し、被害が軽微だった食品売り場など一部店舗を再開する意向を伝えていたことが27日、複数の遺族への取材で分かった。イオン側は「可能であれば12月にも再開を目指したい」と話したという。ある遺族男性には10月、施設運営会社の役員から電話があり、年内に食品売り場などで再開を目指していることが伝えられた。男性は「どこまでできるか分からないが、できれば再開していきたいという感じだった」と受け止めた。再開に向けて遺族の許可を求められたため「構わない」と答えたという。別の遺族男性も10月、同社役員から「全ての条件がそろえば12月半ばにも再開したい」と伝えられたという。この男性も再開を認めた。男性は「イオン側は調査や補償の話など、ちゃんとステップを踏んで進めている。工事や安全確保などのめどが立てば、再開は問題ないと思う」と語った。
施設運営会社の親会社イオン（千葉市）の広報担当者は熊本日日新聞の取材に「（弁護士ら第三者による）事故調査委員会が継続中で、イオンとして店舗の再開について話せる段階ではない」と回答。事故調査に協力し、可能な限り早く結論が得られるよう努めると同時に、遺族への補償の話を進めるとした。（堀江利雅、古東竜之介、横川千夏、上島諒）

title: ニデック 創業者ら9人を提訴へ
body: 京都市に本社があるモーター大手の「ニデック」はきょう＝27日、会計不正の問題を受けて創業者の永守重信氏をはじめ、歴代社長５人を含む旧役員９人に対し、損害賠償を求める訴えを起こすことを決定したと明らかにしました。【関連記事】ニデックが2025年度の決算を発表　6300億円超の減損損失を計上し5646億円の最終赤字ニデックをめぐっては、グループ内で収益を過大に計上したり損失の計上を先延ばしにしたりするなどといった会計不正が複数見つかっています。この問題について、弁護士などでつくる第三者委員会は報告書で、創業者である永守重信氏を起点とする強すぎる業績へのプレッシャーが原因としたうえで、直接的な関与はないものの「会計不正について最も責めを負うべきと言わざるを得ない」と結論付けています。会社は、第三者委の報告書を踏まえ、過去の役員を対象に法的責任の有無を調べるために役員責任調査委員会を設置し調査を行っていましたが、調査委員会は今月16日、創業者である永守氏をはじめ、先月社長を辞任した岸田光哉氏など歴代の社長５人を含む計９人に対し「損害の範囲については寄与度について判断されるべき」としつつ「会社法に基づく損害賠償責任がある」と結論付けています。これを受け、ニデックは「複数の取締役等において、その職務執行に関して法令に違反する事実があったものと認める」として、法的措置の検討を行ってきましたがきょう＝27日、９人を相手取り損害賠償を起こすことを決定したと明らかにしました。具体的には、社長を務めた永守重信氏・小部博志氏・吉本浩之氏・関潤氏・岸田光哉氏の５人のほか、佐藤明氏・村上和也氏・落合裕之氏の旧取締役３人、それに最高財務責任者を務めた旧執行役員の計９人です。会社は９人に対する請求額などを検討し、準備が整い次第、提訴する予定だとしています。

title: 米MS 6万人に退職パッケージ提示
body:
（ブルームバーグ）:ソフトウエア最大手の米マイクロソフトは、約6万人の従業員に退職パッケージを提示する。コスト削減を進めるとともに、AI時代を見据えて人員体制を再構築する取り組みの一環。【写真を見る】マイクロソフト、6万人に退職パッケージ提示-AI対応の再編同社の広報担当者によると、対象となるのは米国、カナダ、インド、英国の一部チームに所属するバイスプレジデント以下の従業員だ。事情に詳しい関係者によると、Xbox、ウィンドウズ、コパイロット、財務などの部門は全面的に対象となる。一方、データセンターや営業、マーケティング、サイバーセキュリティー、量子コンピューティングに携わる一部の従業員は対象外となる。マイクロソフトはこうした詳細についてコメントを控えた。最高人事責任者（CPO）のエイミー・コールマン氏は26日付の従業員向け文書で「社外でのキャリアを検討している人にとって、支援を受けながら転身するという新たな選択肢になる」と説明した。広報担当者によれば、応じた従業員には通常の退職パッケージと同様の給付が提供される。マイクロソフトは近年、数次にわたる人員削減で数万人を減らしてきた。7月には退職年齢に達した従業員を対象に同様のパッケージを提示。約8750人の対象者のうち、30％余りが応じた。ただ、今回のパッケージに応じる従業員は、7月の制度に比べて大幅に少なくなるだろうと広報担当者は述べた。6月末時点のマイクロソフト従業員数は22万3000人だった。AIやデータセンターへの大規模な投資を始めた時期とほぼ重なる2022年以降、従業員数はおおむね横ばいで推移してきた。こうした投資が社内の他部門で、予算や人員採用を圧迫している。同社は28日に決算を発表する予定で、投資家はAIへの巨額投資が成果につながっている兆候が示されるかに強い関心を寄せている。26日の米株式市場で、マイクロソフト株は1.5％高の532.26ドルで引けた。原題:Microsoft to Offer Buyouts to 60,000 Workers in New Cost Cut （1）（抜粋）
（対象部門などの詳細を加え、これまでの経緯と決算発表予定について追記します）もっと読むにはこちら bloomberg.com/jp（c）2026 Bloomberg L.P.
Brody Ford, Nikki Waller

title: 大手生保 国債の入れ替え加速
body: 長期金利の上昇傾向を踏まえ、大手生命保険会社が日本国債の入れ替えを加速させる。低金利時代に買い入れた国債を売却し、利率の高い国債を購入。運用利回りを向上させ、これまでよりも契約者に有利な保険商品を販売する。【ひと目でわかる】日本国債の保有者別割合大手10社は26日までに、2026年度下半期（10月～27年3月）の資産運用計画を発表。9社が3月末時点の長期金利を3％台と見込んだ。日銀の追加利上げについても、多くが今年度中にあと2回実施すると予想した。これらの想定を踏まえ、第一生命保険は償還（払い戻し）までの期間が20～40年の「超長期債」と呼ばれる国債を中心に、年間で約1兆円超入れ替える。明治安田生命保険は入れ替えと新規投資を合わせ、国債を2兆円程度購入する。北村乾一郎運用企画部長は「来年度まで、今の金利水準でかなりの運用資産を入れ替えたい」と述べた。長期金利の上昇は、保有国債の含み損が膨らむことにつながる。日本生命保険は今年4～9月に当初計画を超える1兆1000億円の入れ替えを実施。下半期も同程度を見込む。インフレ圧力や中東情勢の先行き不透明感を背景に、「安全資産」で運用する動きも広がっている。第一生命は今年度から金を組み入れ、今後3年程度で資産全体の約1％まで積み増す方針。富国生命保険は金融市場の流動化に備え、昨年度末までに積み上げた現預金の水準を維持する。

title: たまごの平均価格 最高値を更新
body: 全国の小売店で販売された、たまごの平均価格が最高値を更新しました。また、輸入牛肉と鶏もも肉の価格も最高値に並びました。【卵の全国平均小売価格の推移】2016年は200円台で推移も鳥インフルエンザ再流行や生産コスト上昇などで高値に【画像で見る】農林水産省によりますと、今月19日から21日までに全国の小売店で販売された、たまご1パックあたりの平均価格は312円で、最高値を更新しました。去年発生した鳥インフルエンザの影響が続き、いまも供給量が少なくなっているほか、年末に向けて需要が高まり始めているということです。また、輸入牛肉の平均価格も100グラムあたり451円と、7月につけた最高値に並びました。円安によって輸入価格が上昇していることや、アメリカで発生した干ばつの影響で、牛の飼育頭数が減っていることが影響したとみられます。さらに、牛肉や豚肉の高騰で比較的安い鶏肉の人気が引き続き高まっていて、鶏もも肉の平均価格も100グラムあたり156円と、最高値に並んでいます。

title: Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
summary: An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Finland's President Alexander Stubb said.
body:
Norway and Finland say they are not acting on behalf of other European leaders
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
summary: The truce was originally planned for the stranded residents of Oleshky, and Russia and Ukraine say no breaches have been reported.
body:
The people of Oleshky have had no electricity for years and no access to food or water
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.
Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.
What we know about Ukraine-Russia truce in Oleshky, brokered by Melania Trump
That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.
Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".
A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".
Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.
Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.
One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.
Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".
These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year
The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.
Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".
Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.
Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.
Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped
It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.
Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.
Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".
White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".
He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.
One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".
However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.
Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.
"Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv.

title: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
summary: The France star had referred to the former Chinese leader as a "dictator" during an interview about memes.
body:
A backlash has erupted on Chinese social media over Mbappé's comments on a "Chinese dictator"
Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands.
Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.
The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,"  Mbappé said in a statement.
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."
Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.
A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.
Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé.
The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".
The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".
Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.
But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".
Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".
Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.
Weibo users are recirculating the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to Mao
Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another  comment on Weibo.
As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".
Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement:"Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."
According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.
China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
Mbappé has a significant commercial presence in China
China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with Mbappé, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry.
By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on Mbappé, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with Mbappé" topping the list.
"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo.
Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s.
His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.
His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.
So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past.
Mbappé has said some of the memes "reveal a lack of political and human awareness"
It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online.
Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business.
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname.
France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.
In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people".
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said.
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."
Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond Chia

title: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America
summary: The Trump-Lula relationship may have thawed, but several issues could reignite tensions between the two leaders.
body:
"Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a message squarely aimed at Washington.
Domestic elections are rarely won on foreign policy, and this one was no different. But Lula's defiance against what he has described as US interference in Brazilian affairs evoked a patriotic spirit that proved an effective campaigning tool.
It also chimed with his wider brand of politics as a former union leader: standing up to powerful figures.
Paradoxically, it seems to have earned him President Donald Trump's respect. "I like Lula, we get along well," Trump said, responding to the result. "I didn't take sides," he added, before calling the election "terrible" and "rigged".
Watch: How President Lula turned it around to beat Flávio Bolsonaro
If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who refused to recognise the result. But Trump was a close ally of Flávio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.
When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which theUS president called a "witch-hunt".
Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back – and it paid off.
He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians".
His approval ratings jumped.
He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic – a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain.
Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.
The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again.
Relations then improved.
The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied".
Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strong leader.
Fireworks heard after Lula's victory in São Paulo
So why might Trump be unhappy with the result?
Latin America has swung to the right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru all electing presidents closely aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has sought to use these allies to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere, a strategy he has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine".
Christopher Sabatini, senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, notes that Trump thought Brazil would be the "10th and biggest prize" after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round.
Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and the younger Bolsonaro was expected to join Trump's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking.
Brazil also holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China, and the US had been eyeing preferential access.
The relationship has thawed, but with four more years ahead for Lula, several issues could reignite tensions.
Brazil accused the US earlier this year of trying to cast doubt on its electoral system and denied visas to two state department officials planning to visit.
The US called this "baseless" and revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa in response.
If Trump keeps calling this result "rigged", further diplomatic fallout is likely.
Lula has also vehemently opposed US military action in the region, from the seizure of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela to the bombing of alleged drug-trafficking vessels.
He lambasted Washington for designating Brazil's two major gangs as terrorist organisations after lobbying from Flávio Bolsonaro, and warned of attacks on Brazilian sovereignty.
It is a sensitive subject for a political left that remembers the region's brutal 20th Century dictatorships, many backed by the CIA in the name of stopping communism.
Then there is US tech.
Lula's campaign accused Meta of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro.
Meta denied this but admitted moderation issues and technical errors had wrongly removed some posts or limited their reach.
Lula's supporters responded by sharing his messages through a 10-million-strong WhatsApp group to bypass the algorithms.
Separately, the Trump administration is unhappy with Pix, Brazil's instant payment system, which has boosted the economy, but which the US sees as taking business from Visa and Mastercard.
The relationship has exposed political divisions.
In the campaign, Bolsonaro supporters waved US flags at their rallies and, in one case, an inflatable saying "Trump Nuke Brazil", while Lula and his supporters accused Flávio Bolsonaro of protecting US interests over Brazil's.
Still, tensions can be overstated.
The US remains Brazil's second-biggest trading partner after China, and for now the two leaders get on.
Whether that lasts will depend on how far the US tries to intervene in Brazilian affairs, and how bullish Lula is in response.
Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again

title: Dutch zookeeper dies after being mauled by leopard
summary: The woman began her career at the park when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.
body:
An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.
The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.
She sustained injuries to her head and neck and had emergency surgery, but the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.
An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.
Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.
"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.
The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.
Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injuries she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition.
A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.
"They are, and remain, predators."
Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.

title: I get £4,062 a year and am trying my best - here's what I want from the Budget
summary: People on a range of incomes from £4,062 to £150,000 a year tell the BBC what they want to see in this year's Budget.
body:
Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the Budget
Chancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.
Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".
BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.
If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch viaBBC Your Voice.
Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.
The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.
"I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."
She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government'sJobs Guarantee,externalscheme extended.
The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.
She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."
Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.
He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.
He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."
The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.
"The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."
The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, and the BBC understands it will be frozen again, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase
Healey pledges cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package of 'everyday fixes'
Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.
Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.
"Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."
Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.
He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently.
He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announceda scheme to help first-time buyers in Englandwho have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."
Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living.
She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."
She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.
"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."
Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.
But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, the £250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.
Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as £50.
Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families.
"I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."
Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.
His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.
"I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."
More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors.
"If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."
Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her.
"It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."
Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look atremoving standing charges from gas bills, Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.
She would also like the government to extend access topension credit,external, a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.
She was unconvinced byAndy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lockso that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".
Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".

title: Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase
summary: Chancellor John Healey will reveal the new pay rates in the Budget, and has also announced measures to help households with the cost of living.
body:
The rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget, but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.
Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.
However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage.
Chancellor John Healey is also announcing measures to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living.
"The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time," Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the BBC:
"Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account."
The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from £10.85 an hour to around £11.27.
That is a smaller rise than the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place for younger workers since returning to power in 2024.
Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage for older workers, which is currently £12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to £13.20, the Times said.
Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job.
"Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally."
The government has also announced a number of measures, including removing import taxes on some food and ending the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments.
It says removing tariffs from 100 food items could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June.
"We're not going to say it is everything," Reynolds told the BBC, but taken alongside the changes implemented in the summer on goods such as pasta, fruit juice and tuna, he said it would save around £500m a year.
Other measures the government announced on Tuesday included:
Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that
Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030
Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period
And rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easier
Speaking to the BBC's Newscast, Healey said: "None of this is going to change the world. But if it helps around the margins and its action the government can take, then I want try and fix it."
The government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands. The 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since.

The list of products the government is removing tariffs on includes:
Chocolate-coated wafers and waffles
Toffees, caramels and similar sweets
Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes
Throat pastilles and cough drops
Plant-based drinks including soya, nut, cereal or seed
The government said removing tariffs on fertiliser aimed to help farmers, while changes to import levies on kerosene is targeted at households that rely on heating oil.
The Treasury said it would publish on Wednesday a full list of the products that will have tariffs removed.
A tariff is an import duty paid by domestic businesses buying products from overseas.
Asked why the government was making it cheaper to buy goods from abroad rather than cutting business costs for UK firms, Reynolds said: "Where you can make a reduction in the cost of importing goods into the UK, when you think you can balance that with your domestic economic interests, that's a decision we will take."
But Balwinder Dhoot, director of sustainability and growth at the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said: "It's more expensive to make food and drink here in the UK than in many of our close neighbours, as businesses face such high energy costs."
The Conservatives said the government's "everyday fixes" had already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
body:
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.
Official data released in the last week,externalshow the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestoneas China grapples with an ageing populationthat could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and forcouples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.
The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
Birth rates in China have been falling for years now
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversialone-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.
The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.
Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.
The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

title: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiar
summary: Donald Trump heads into the US midterm elections with an issue similar to his political foe Joe Biden.
body:
US President Donald Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden
The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is.
It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them.
Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge.
During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices.
"When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said.
Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected.
Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs.
Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know:prices remain high.
The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies.
The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills.
US economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall.
Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working.
Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis".
Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as"the greatest story never told",external, arguing that "nobody is getting fired".
US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
But voters appear to be reading a different story - one in which Trump won the presidency promising to tackle the cost of living, only for prices to keep rising.
Part of the problem is that wage increases have not kept pace with prices. Average hourly earnings have risen 3% over the last year, while consumer prices have increased 3.7%.
That helps explain why polls continue to show voters giving Trump poor marks for his handling of the economy.
For Democrats, the dynamic feels familiar.
Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, says the problem begins with the way economists and voters use the same language to mean different things.
"When economists say inflation comes down, they mean the rate of increase has come down," she says.
"When voters say inflation has come down, they mean the price has returned to what it was. Well, of course, it never returns to what it was."
Joe Biden campaigned in 2024 on the economy but voters saw things differently
The Biden administration spent much of 2024 highlighting low unemployment, solid growth and falling inflation. However, many voters remained focused on the higher prices they faced every day.
Lake, who advised Biden's 2020 campaign but was not involved in the 2024 race, says voters judge the economy through personal experience, not economic indicators.
"You can't argue with people about their own lived reality," she says.
That may help explain why Trump's challenge looks so similar to Biden's.
Biden's critics blamed him for inflation. But he could point to forces largely outside his control, including the pandemic and its supply chain aftershocks.
Trump has less room to do that.
Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of his own policies, including tariffs, as well as the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran.
"The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans.
"It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it."
Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers.
A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%.
Donald Trump pledged to lower prices for US households
The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.
Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets.
The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures.
Trump has called fora cap on credit card interest ratesand floated the idea ofa $5,000 payment to American adultsif Republicans retain control of Congress.
The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough.
Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can.
If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself.

title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
summary: Figures obtained by BBC Newsnight show large spikes in sales of torches, radios and power banks.
body:
UK prepper stores see massive sales following government campaign
Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.
The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.
The rise in sales cameafter Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saidthat people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.
Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.
The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.
"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.
"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."
On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.
Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.
In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."
An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."
Sales of torches and radio have risen sharply for some UK retailers
Newsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.
Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing – order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."
Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."

title: Chris Mason: Budget needs to go some way towards delivering PM's promises
summary: Support on the cost of living, and in particular energy bills, as well as announcments on devolution will be central to John Healey's first Budget.
body:
Two quotes from the chancellor and the prime minister get to the heart of this Budget.
"The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there now… Britain has it harder now," Chancellor John Healey said last month.
And from Andy Burnham, days before he became prime minister: "This change... is the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years."
So what happens when the economic realities confront the political ambitions of this new government?
As Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS),puts it,external: "We have a relatively new government with seemingly big ambitions but facing a long list of constraints.
"Some of those constraints… are self imposed, others are being worsened by global events, most noticeably war in the Middle East."
Let's be clear, plenty in Westminster in all parties will say that the amount of money around isn't everything – how well taxpayers' money is spent and where it is spent matters too.
And spending less and taxing less, plenty argue, should be a priority.
But in the bones of many in the Labour Party is an instinct that the government, the state, can and should be a vital agent in driving change and improvements in people's lives – a world-view grounded in a sense that governments should proudly step in, rather than one that believes they should get out of the way.
And how do you deliver a proudly proactive state, delivering for people in a noticeable way, when the tax burden is generationally high, the national debt is sky high,energy bills are risingand inflation is higher than expected?
In short: it is not easy.
Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase
Tax on banks, energy bill help and minimum wage rise - what could be in the Budget?
Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds
But ministers argue all of this doesn't mean the government is powerless.
Many are expecting support on the cost of living, and in particular energy bills, to be targeted at the most vulnerable. On the eve of the Budget, Healey said he wants to "start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good".
Thebanks are braced for a levy or surchargethat may pay for this.
There will be an announcement about further spending on defence, but not yet how spending 3% of national income on our security will be delivered by 2030 – that will come in next year's Spending Review.
And one of the prime minister's key ideas - handing power away from Westminster and closer to you, devolution - will be central too.
There will be, the chancellor told BBC Newscast, a "really radical devolution of powers and resources to local leaders that are often better placed to get beyond the departmental systems."
But some at Westminster fret extra money for mayors and others in local government are not yet accompanied by adequate checks and balances to ensure that money is well spent.
The chancellor will argue the economy is becoming more robust – and yes, there are some economic indicators that are more positive than forecast: growth is better than expected, as is productivity and unemployment is down.
But as theResolution Foundation think tank points out,external: "John Healey's problem is that conflict in the Middle East has once again pushed up energy prices and interest rates.
"So, despite the signs that the UK economy is becoming more resilient, household and public finances are in for another shock."
Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
In essence, we can expect a smaller Budget this time, compared to some in recent years, when it comes to the scale of tax and spending changes.
The chancellor has been talking up a desire to offer "breathing space" and "hope" - a tacit acknowledgement that there is a limit to what the government can do given the constraints it faces.
It has promised not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT, a self imposed constraint, as the IFS put it. And there are the international ones beyond its control too.
The big question for many will be whether the Budget is – or can be - big enough to meet the moment? Opposition parties will argue it amounts to tinkering.
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith argued the public finances are "on a cliff edge" and wants Healey to use the Budget to "take tough decisions, instead of continuing to kick the can down the road".
For the Liberal Democrats, Daisy Cooper warned a "steady as she goes" Budget is "not going to cut it", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said the chancellor "can't keep fiddling while the economy burns".
Green Party MP Ellie Chowns wanted a "bold" approach but fears it will be "business as usual".
The government will try to convince you it is one of many moments in the coming weeks and months that will attempt to deliver the scale of change the prime minister has promised.

The list of products the government is removing tariffs on includes:
Chocolate-coated wafers and waffles
Toffees, caramels and similar sweets
Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes
Throat pastilles and cough drops
Plant-based drinks including soya, nut, cereal or seed
The government said removing tariffs on fertiliser aimed to help farmers, while changes to import levies on kerosene is targeted at households that rely on heating oil.
The Treasury said it would publish on Wednesday a full list of the products that will have tariffs removed.
A tariff is an import duty paid by domestic businesses buying products from overseas.
Asked why the government was making it cheaper to buy goods from abroad rather than cutting business costs for UK firms, Reynolds said: "Where you can make a reduction in the cost of importing goods into the UK, when you think you can balance that with your domestic economic interests, that's a decision we will take."
But Balwinder Dhoot, director of sustainability and growth at the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said: "It's more expensive to make food and drink here in the UK than in many of our close neighbours, as businesses face such high energy costs."
The Conservatives said the government's "everyday fixes" had already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
summary: Officials are expected to begin discussions on a range of options for the future UK-EU relationship before a summit next month.
body:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds says no "assumptions" have been made about what the future UK-EU relationship could look like
British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told the BBC.
Officials on both sides are expected to begin discussions about a range of options, including free movement, before the EU summit on 20 November.
However, Downing Street has insisted the government's current focus is on achieving new deals in areas such as food and youth mobility at the summit.
Reynolds said no "assumptions" had been made about what the UK's future relationship with Brussels could look like.
Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion"about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.
But the prime minister has been clear any major changes to the UK-EU relationship would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.
He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.
Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.
The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.
No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days
Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.
He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.
"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.
"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."
Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.
"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."
A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.
"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.
Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.
Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.
But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.
Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.
"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.
Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."
Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."
Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.
On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.
The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.
But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his ownwhen he told the Sunday Times,externalthat he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.
The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.
